source.title: Challenging the Scale Paradigm: Small Language Models in Multi-Agent Architectures for Enterprise Business Intelligence
source.authors: Cassiano Moralles; L. A. D. da Costa; Éderson Passos Silva; George Lucas Ebertz Prado; Taimisson de Carvalho Schardosim; S. Rigo; Rafael Kunst; Vinícius Costa De Souza; A. Roehrs

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares downstream task success across differently sized models, a different measure from pretraining loss, and reports whether task performance changes with model size.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or sweep training tokens or compute, and it does not fit or extrapolate power laws or test compute-optimal allocations. Scaling-law findings from other work appear only as background citations. The multi-agent comparisons concern agent configuration and count, not a model-size scaling sweep.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates seven existing models (1B–30B) on 30 BI tasks and compares task success across sizes, so it bears on V6 in a new setting. But every model scored 100%, so the measure is at ceiling from the smallest model up. The models are also not a controlled scaling series: different families, a fine-tuned variant, and quantization above 8B. The success criterion is never defined. The data therefore cannot show whether performance tracks scale.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that for structured BI tasks success saturates at about 1B parameters, with larger models adding cost and latency (up to 44× token-seconds) without success gains. They also conclude that deeper multi-agent pipelines degrade success (down to 50%) through error propagation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates task success across existing models of different sizes; it does not train models across parameter, token, or compute scales or fit loss scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: In multi-agent pipelines, success fell to 50% for the 7-model Full-Spectrum configuration versus 100% for 2-agent SLM setups (Fig. 1, Sec. 4.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing agent count in sequential LLM pipelines does not improve, and can degrade, task success. This is a scaling-of-agents question, not model scale.

record.code_released: The authors state that code, prompts, and experimental configurations will be made publicly available upon publication; no URL is stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Anais do XVIII Simpósio Brasileiro de Computação Ubíqua e Pervasiva (SBCUP 2026)
record.problems: The evidence for the tested downstream-performance comparison is limited to structured business-intelligence tasks. The paper notes use of a single 8GB GPU and quantization for models above 8B, which may bias comparisons; it does not report uncertainty for the per-model success rates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the multi-agent configurations: those comparisons vary agent count and composition rather than model size in the sense tested by V6. Latency, token-seconds, and energy results do not measure the outcomes named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Any task not saturated by a 1B model. Any relation of task performance to pretraining loss. Any controlled model-size series within one family.

missing.what: Definition of task success (scoring method, judge, criteria) behind the 100% figures

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is given because the rows cannot discriminate. A uniform 100% across 1B–30B is a ceiling effect on easy, undefined-criterion tasks, and it is not evidence that V6 is absent. Further confounds are mixed model families, quantization only for the larger models (acknowledged as possibly favouring small models), and 512-token output caps. The record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' applies only to latency and token-seconds statistics; no uncertainty is given for success rates. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Power-law fits on small runs and predictions of larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper tests task success across model sizes only on structured business-intelligence tasks; it does not relate performance to pretraining loss or test broader downstream task domains.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, or departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: Google Gemma-3-1B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated success on the business-intelligence task set.
rows.note: The paper states that all seven evaluated models achieved this success rate across all 30 tasks.
rows.check: Ceiling: 100% for all seven models, so the measure cannot show improvement with scale. The success criterion and judge are not described.

reader_labels.reason: Task success was 100% for every model, so this setting showed saturation rather than increasing performance with model size (r1–r7).
